name: Olga Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at the Redhill copper pit, one of the big ones, a 220-tonne truck that's taller than my house. A day shift starts with the prestart at quarter to six: walk around the truck, check the tyres, the lights, the fire suppression, sign the sheet. Then it's twelve hours of loading under the shovel, crawling up the ramp full, tipping at the crusher, and coming back down empty, maybe thirty loads if nothing breaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same every day and I know what's expected. The crew's good, my union rep Daniela looks out for the juniors, and the pay is better than anything else I could get with just school behind me. What wears me out is the night roster, and that I'm still slow on the tight spots at the dump. The trainer, Gus, still rides along sometimes and I hate that, but he's right, I'm not there yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the crib room: told you so. Every year somebody says the computers are coming for us and every year I'm still in the cab. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would be a relief. I've only been doing this two years and I'm still learning the job, so I'd like it to just stay put long enough for me to get good at it. If nothing changes, I keep the roster, the pay and the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep putting a third of every pay into savings like I do now, keep paying my union dues, and keep asking Gus for extra time on the dump practice. Maybe I'd finally book the trip to see my aunt that I keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather warning that turns out to be a light shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned savings. How much have you put away, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fourteen months of my costs, which sounds like a lot but my rent is cheap because I share a flat with my partner, Tomas. My mum always said miners get laid off in a bust, so you save in a boom. I don't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that would still bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The automated trucks over at the Kestrel pit, the ones already running with no driver. Even if AI is hype, those are real and they were there before all this AI talk. So even in the quiet version, I'd still keep one eye on Kestrel.

S0.say: I'd tell people in the crib room and the union chat that I told them so. Every year somebody says computers are coming for us and I'm still in the cab.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I'm still learning the job and want it to stay put long enough for me to get good at it. If nothing changes I keep the roster, the pay and the crew.
S0.do: Keeps putting a third of each pay into savings and keeps paying union dues. Asks her trainer for extra practice at the dump and might finally book a trip to see her aunt.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with a small worry about the driverless trucks already running at the next pit.
S0.quote: Even if AI is hype, those are real and they were there before all this AI talk.
S0.fieldNote: Olga is a junior haul truck driver who wants the world to hold still while she learns. Her calm here rests on solid savings and the union. The one thing that cuts through it is the driverless fleet at the neighbouring pit, which she treats as a separate, older threat from AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union in the room before any of it happens, not after. At work I'd be the one pushing for a meeting with Daniela. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers, not the company's shiny brochures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my truck is the first thing on the list. Driving a haul truck up and down a ramp is the easiest thing in the whole pit to hand to a computer, and I know it. The older drivers have skills to fall back on, and I don't yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go to every union meeting and ask for a written promise that no driver gets cut without being offered another job on site. I'd stop the trip and any big spending and push my savings higher. I wouldn't sign up for the remote control course they'd offer, not unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, more a knot in the stomach every time I drive past Kestrel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not the remote control course? It might keep you on site.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's sitting in a dark room in front of six screens watching trucks that used to have people in them. I didn't come to the mine to work in an office. And I'm bad with computers, I don't even use those AI chat things, so I'd be starting at the bottom again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if your truck goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, and the shareholders who want another cent on the dividend. The machines don't decide anything, people decide to buy them and not share what they save. If the mine makes more money with fewer of us, some of that should come back to the town.

S1.say: I'd say this is why the union needs to be in the room before any change, not after. I'd push for a meeting at work and share things about protecting workers online.
S1.think: I think my haul truck is first on the list, because driving up and down a ramp is the easiest job in the pit to hand to a computer. Older drivers have other skills and I don't yet.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting and pushes for a written promise of redeployment for drivers. Cancels her trip, raises her savings rate, and avoids signing up for the remote operations course unless forced.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a knot in the stomach whenever she drives past the automated pit.
S1.quote: I didn't come to the mine to work in an office. And I'm bad with computers, I don't even use those AI chat things
S1.fieldNote: Her answer to change is the union, not the training room. She sees clearly that her own job is the most exposed in the pit, yet turns down the obvious route to stay, because it means screens instead of a cab. She puts the blame squarely on owners who don't share the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that nobody stopped it, and that the government let a handful of companies decide for everyone. I'd be at whatever protest the union organised, with a sign. Online I'd be angry, I won't pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm out. Two years in, still learning, in the most automatable seat in the mine. If robots can do hands-on work too, I can't even go and drive a truck somewhere else, because every mine would do the same thing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, straight away, and keep every cent of the fourteen months. I'd go to the union and to the local member of parliament, and push hard for some kind of payment for workers who get pushed out. I'd probably move in with my mum for a while to make the money last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground going soft under the truck. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in those two years that you wouldn't do otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly, and that scares me. Two years isn't enough to learn a trade properly, and anyway, which trade? I'd just hold onto the job as long as they let me, save like mad, and get loud with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with your mum. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back in my old bedroom at twenty-eight, with Tomas on a mattress if he came. Mum would be kind about it but she'd also say she warned me about mining. That bit would sting more than losing the truck.

S2.say: I'd call it a disgrace that the government let a few companies decide for everyone. I'd join any union protest and be openly angry online.
S2.think: It means I'm out, two years in and sitting in the most automatable seat in the mine. If robots do hands-on work everywhere, I can't just drive a truck at another mine.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food at once and protects her fourteen months of savings. Lobbies through the union and her local member of parliament for payments to displaced workers, and plans to move back in with her mum to stretch the money.
S2.feel: Frightened and angry, losing sleep, like the ground going soft under the truck.
S2.quote: Back in my old bedroom at twenty-eight, with Tomas on a mattress if he came.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her savings stop feeling like protection and start feeling like a countdown. She has no plan beyond holding on and getting loud, and she admits two years is too short to retrain. The sharpest pain is not the job but her mother's I-told-you-so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to make rules, not just watch. I'd be pushing the union to fight for retraining paid by the company, on company time. I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending, just slower. Five years would get me to being a good truck driver, right at the moment nobody needs one. That's a bit of a joke when you say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, and in the first couple of years I'd make myself look at other trades, maybe something like an electrician, even though I hate the idea of school again. I'd get on the union's committee for the change, if they'd have someone junior. When it arrives, I'd lean on the union deal and my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. There's at least a bit of room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether the union can actually win anything. In two years nobody can organise, it's over before the first meeting. In five you can get a deal on paper, things like notice periods and retraining money, and that matters more to me than anything I could do on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at electrician work. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look, I'd probably go to the open day, and then I'd likely talk myself out of it. I'm not good at starting over. If the union got the company to pay and Daniela was doing it too, maybe.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to make rules instead of just watching. I'd push the union to fight for retraining paid by the company and sign every petition.
S3.think: It's the same ending, just slower. Five years would make me a good truck driver right when nobody needs one.
S3.do: Keeps driving and saving while reluctantly looking at trades such as electrical work. Tries to join the union's committee on the changes, and plans to rely on a union deal and her savings when the change arrives.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with some room to breathe.
S3.quote: Five years would get me to being a good truck driver, right at the moment nobody needs one.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time matters to her almost entirely as time for the union to win a deal, not time for her to change. She is honest that she'd probably talk herself out of retraining unless others went with her. Her dependence on the group is both her strength and her trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. That would be my line at work and online. A decade means the company and the government can plan, and we should make them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels further away than it is. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd probably tell myself it's fine for a long time and then panic in year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep driving, keep saving, and keep paying my dues. I'd get the union to push for the company to fund apprenticeships on site. I don't think I'd do much else in the first year, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anything. It's far off, but I know myself, and I know I'd leave it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd panic in year eight. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me at the kitchen table with Tomas, printing off job ads at midnight. Him saying he told me so in year two. I can see it already, which is a bit sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version that sounds good to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that by then we'd have rules, so people aren't just thrown out. And if Tomas and I wanted kids, there'd be time to sort out money first. But I don't want a robot in my truck, ten years or not.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so nobody should be left behind. The company and the government can plan, and we should make them.
S4.think: Ten years feels further off than it is, and I'd be thirty-seven. I'd tell myself it's fine for ages and then panic in year eight.
S4.do: Keeps driving, saving and paying union dues in the first year. Pushes the union to get the company to fund on-site apprenticeships, but admits she would do little else at first.
S4.feel: Uneasy, knowing her own habit of leaving things late.
S4.quote: Me at the kitchen table with Tomas, printing off job ads at midnight.
S4.fieldNote: The decade-long version is the one where she is most self-aware: she predicts her own delay. The longer runway lowers her fear but not her resistance to changing seats. She'd use the time to press for rules rather than to move herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because there's no time for the union to do anything. What would help is a real deal: notice, a payment for every year you worked, and retraining that's paid and done on site with people you know. I'm not going to go to some college in the city on my own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Half the shops on Bridge Street live off our wages. If the trucks drive themselves, the bakery goes, the pub goes, and nobody in head office will even notice.

headlineQuote: If the trucks drive themselves, the bakery goes, the pub goes, and nobody in head office will even notice.
portrait: Olga Novak is a 27-year-old haul truck driver at a large copper pit, two years into the job and still learning the tight spots at the dump. She lives with her partner Tomas, saves a third of every pay, and has about fourteen months of costs put away. She is a committed union member who avoids computers and has never used an AI tool. She moves from relief in the quiet scenario to real alarm when AGI arrives in two years, and in every version her answer is the union and her savings rather than retraining herself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for the union to win anything before her truck was taken over.
whatWouldHelp: A real deal with notice, a payment for every year worked, and paid retraining done on site with people she knows.
